title: Just ask
hook: du'a is asking Allah directly, any time, in any language

segments.voice: Yesterday: qurbani, the sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, shared three ways. Your line was a third for the poor. Did one plate, or one third of something, leave your hands? Day one hundred thirty.

For weeks now, this path has been teaching forms. The exact words of the prayer, in Arabic. Where the hands go. How many times to say glory. How many units at dawn. It can start to feel like there's a correct way to do everything, and a wrong way to be avoided. So here's a relief. There's one kind of prayer in Islam that has no required form at all. No set words. No set language. No set time. You don't even need to be facing anywhere. You just talk. Today: just ask.
screen: `WEEKS OF EXACT FORMS.` → `ONE PRAYER WITH NO FORM AT ALL.` → `YOU JUST TALK.`

segments.voice: The word is du'a, from an Arabic root that means to call, the way you'd call someone's name across a room. The salat, the five daily prayers, is the fixed form: set times, set movements, set words in Arabic. Du'a is the open one. Asking Allah for something, directly, whenever you want. In Arabic, in English, in Urdu, in the half-sentences you'd use at three in the morning. Most scholars say you don't need wudu for it, or a prayer mat, or a particular direction, though many people like to face the qiblah and raise their hands. The Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, gave it a surprising rank. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report him saying: du'a is worship itself. And then he recited a verse, Surah Ghafir, forty, sixty: And your Lord hath said: Pray unto Me and I will hear your prayer. Not a formal request through the proper office. Pray unto Me. What about the times it seems nothing happens? The hadith collections are honest about that. Bukhari reports that a person's du'a is answered as long as they don't grow impatient and say, I prayed and prayed and nothing came. And a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad says every sincere du'a is answered in one of three ways: given now, saved for the next life, or a harm of the same size quietly turned away. So a du'a is never wasted. It may just come back in a shape you didn't order. Which leaves only the hard part: actually asking.
screen: `DU'A — TO CALL.` · `SALAT IS FIXED; DU'A IS OPEN.` · `DU'A IS WORSHIP ITSELF.` · `ANSWERED IN ONE OF THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `JUST ASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one thing plainly. Sit comfortably. Take a breath, and let it out slowly. Now find the thing you actually want, not the polite version. Maybe it's small: sleep, a good conversation tomorrow, the test results. Maybe it's large. Put it into one plain sentence. If you pray, you can say it to Allah, in any language, out loud or silently. If you don't, just say the sentence to yourself and notice how it feels to admit you want it. Then sit with it, and don't add anything. The bell holds the time.
Du'a. Calling on Allah directly, any time, in any language, asking for what you need. Today's word.
Your line: just ask. Somewhere today, you'll catch yourself worrying about something. When you do, turn the worry into one plain sentence of asking, and leave it there. Day one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Muslims make du'a at any time and in any language, often after the salat or with hands raised, asking Allah directly for their own needs and for others.

fork.setup: you've asked for the same thing for months, and nothing seems to change. what does the hadith in Bukhari warn against?
options: growing impatient and saying 'I prayed and nothing came'
fork.reveal: a du'a is answered as long as the person doesn't grow impatient and give up (Bukhari). the warning is about quitting, not about how you ask.

original.note: Arabic: calling, supplication, from the root d-'-w, to call.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslim prayer is all set words in Arabic.
what it means: the salat is fixed, but du'a is open: any time, any language, your own words.
what a scholar hears: 'du'a is worship' (Abu Dawud 1479; Tirmidhi 2969), followed by 40:60; and the three answers (Ahmad).
